title: Most People in Japan Still Value Handwriting
paragraphs: From messages and shopping lists to schoolwork and office documents, much of what we write today is typed on a screen.
But people in Japan are still putting pen to paper. A new government survey has found that nearly 70% of people write by hand in their day-to-day lives.

The survey was done by Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs, which has been asking people about the Japanese language every year since 1995. More than 3,500 people aged 16 and older took part in the latest survey.
The results show that many people care about writing by hand, with eight in 10 saying that it should be preserved.
Handwritten messages are especially popular. When asked about letters and postcards, 82% said they preferred ones that were handwritten.

For the first time, the survey also asked about vertical text — the traditional way of writing Japanese that has become less common as more writing is done on screens. Still, 67% of people said they had opportunities to read or write vertically, and six in 10 said vertical writing should be preserved.
Interestingly, 16- to 19-year-olds were the age group most likely to support preserving both handwriting and vertical writing.
And interest in the Japanese language is growing, too. Over 80% of people said they were interested in Japanese, up around 10 percentage points from the year 2000.
The agency said that social media may be one reason for this, as people now have more opportunities to write for large audiences.
